NOTE:  PUBLIC PARTICIPATION INFORMATION
  In accordance with Assembly Bill 361 (AB 361), City Council Resolution Nos. 2487, 2490, 2491, 2493,
  2498, 2499, 2503, 2505, and proposed Resolution No. 2507, due to the continuing state of emergency,
  including masking and social distancing directives as a result of the threat of the COVID -19 virus, this
  meeting is being broadcast via teleconference. Members of the public may participate in-person in the
  Council Chambers, or virtually in the meeting in the following ways:

  - Members of the public may listen to the meeting live by calling: (1 669 900 6833) from any phone,
  Meeting ID: 892 7403 6356 Meeting Password: 066081. (Please note you will not have the ability to
  speak using the call in option from a phone line.)

  - Public correspondence may be emailed to the City Clerk at laurenp@rollinghillsestatesca.gov. Emails
  received before 3:00 p.m. prior to the start of the meeting will be forwarded to the City Council for their
  consideration and included as part of the record.

  - Members of the public may also comment online using eComment on the “Meeting Agendas, Minutes &
  Videos” page of the City’s website (www.rhe.city/MeetingAgendas). Once the agenda is published, there
  will be an “eComment” button next to the linked agenda under "Upcoming Events". Follow this link to
  the City’s SpeakUp page. After you register, you may comment on any item on that particular agenda.
  These comments can be seen by the public, will be considered by the Council and become part of the
  record.

  - Members of the public who wish to speak during this meeting may join the Zoom meeting by accessing the
  Zoom app from a computer (downloaded at Zoom.com) or tablet or phone (downloaded in the App Store),
  by entering the following credentials: Meeting ID: 892 7403 6356, Meeting Password: 066081. Members
  of the public who join the Zoom meeting will not have video, and may request to speak using the following
  process: After joining the Zoom meeting, if you wish to speak, please select the "raise hand" option at the
  lower portion of your screen. The City Clerk will send you a chat message to identify which item on the
  agenda you would like to speak on and will unmute your mic at the appropriate time.

  Agenda reports and other disclosable public records relating to each Open Session agenda item are
  available on the City's website under Meeting Agendas, Minutes & Videos at www.rhe.city.

MINUTES
  CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  MAY 24, 2022

1.  ALL MEETING TO ORDER

A regular meeting of the City Council of the City of Rolling Hills Estates was called to order
by MAYOR ZERUNYAN at 7:00 p.m. in the Council Chambers of City Hall and remotely via
teleconference, in accordance with Assembly Bill 361 (AB 361) and City Council Resolution
Nos. 2487, 2490, 2491, 2493, 2498, 2499, 2503, 2505 and 2507 due to the continuing state of
emergency, including masking and social distancing directives as a result of the threat of the
COVID-19 virus.

2.  SALUTE TO THE FLAG
Led by students from Peninsula High School – Kick Ash Coalition Club.

Linus Yeh, President of Kick Ash Coalition Club and Ryan Paillet, Vice President of Kick Ash at
Peninsula High School and the Department of Health Services (DHS) introduced themselves and
stated that they are advocating for a smoke-free environment in the City.

3.  ROLL CALL
City Council Members Present:  Zuckerman, Stegura, Huff, Zerunyan

City Council Members Absent:  Schmitz

City Staff Present:  City Manager Greg Grammer
  City Attorney Don Davis
  Administrative Services Director Mike Whitehead
  Community Development & PW Director David Wahba
  Planning Manager Jeannie Naughton
  Administrative Aide Gabby Swain
  City Clerk Lauren Pettit

4.  CEREMONIAL

A.  PROCLAMATION: DECLARING MAY 31, 2022 "WORLD NO TOBACCO DAY"

MAYOR ZERUNYAN declared May 31, 2022 “World No Tobacco Day”,and presented the
Proclamation to the students from Kick Ash.

B.  WASTE MANAGEMENT "RECYCLING HERO" DRAWING FOR ONE YEAR OF FREE
  RESIDENTIAL AND COMMERCIAL REFUSE SERVICE - SECOND QUARTER 2022

Erick Quintero, Waste Management Representative presented a virtual drawing for one year
of free service for a residential customer and announced the commercial customer winner.

Residential Winner: 5133 Elmdale Drive
Commercial Winner: The Jack Kramer Club, 11 Montecillo Drive

5.  CONSENT CALENDAR

The following routine matters will be acted upon by one vote to approve with the majority
consent of the City Council. There will be no separate discussion of these items unless good
cause is shown by a member prior to the roll call vote. (Items removed for individual
consideration will be voted on separately.)

MAYOR PRO TEM HUFF moved, seconded by COUNCIL MEMBER STEGURA, TO
APPROVE CONSENT CALENDAR ITEMS 5A-I AS FOLLOWS BY THE FOLLOWING ROLL
CALL VOTE:
AYES:  Zuckerman, Stegura, Huff, Zerunyan
ABSENT:  Schmitz

MAY 24, 2022

  CONSIDERATION TO THE CITY COUNCIL WILL BE WAIVED AND ALL SUCH
  ORDINANCES AND RESOLUTIONS WILL BE READ BY TITLE ONLY.

6.  PUBLIC COMMENT / PUBLIC PRESENTATIONS

A.  SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA EDISON WILDFIRE MITIGATION PLAN 2022 UPDATE

Southern California Edison representatives Constance Turner, Jae Lee, Ajay Singh and Robert
Brambila provided a Circuit Reliability Review presentation.

MAYOR ZERUNYAN stated that the number of outages has improved substantially within the
last year.

COUNCIL MEMBER STEGURA concurred with the Mayor’s statement and commented that
the presentation addressed the risk of wildfires and how they are being mitigated throughout

CITY COUNCIL MINUTES  2
MAY 24, 2022
 their district, and asked what is being done specifically for the safety of residents of Rolling
Hills Estates.

Ms. Turner stated that money is being invested to reinforce infrastructure and make it stronger
and more fire resistant to prevent as many fires as possible.

COMMITTEE MEMBER STEGURA inquired about the helicopter inspections and if problems
have been identified or if the equipment is to their satisfaction in the area.

Ms. Turner stated that helicopters, drones, and ground inspections are done on a daily basis
in order to identify problems and replace and upgrade equipment.

MAYOR PRO TEM HUFF stated that within the past year there has been increased high winds
in the area and asked if they have noticed an increase in incidents due to the winds.

Ms. Turner stated that the winds always impact the system.

COUNCIL MEMBER ZUCKERMAN inquired about replacing the City’s older transformers.

Ms. Turner stated that this is an ongoing process and replacement depends on various factors,
including their use, transformer failure, load, and age.

COUNCIL MEMBER ZUCKERMAN asked if all of the aluminum conductors have been
removed from the distribution system in the city.

Ms. Turner stated that all the aluminum transformers have been removed.

MAYOR ZERUNYAN inquired about data on the amount of wire that has been changed to
covered conductor in the city.

Ms. Turner stated that the data is not available by City, but rather by circuit; she stated that
she will look into providing the data by the circuits running through the city.

MAYOR ZERUNYAN stated that it would be helpful for the community to know the data on the
work that is being done in the city.

Ms. Turner stated that she will look into this and will get back to staff.

7.  PUBLIC HEARINGS

A.  INTRODUCTION OF ORDINANCE NO. 741 AMENDING AND RESTATING
  MUNICIPAL CODE CHAPTER 17.60 (SIGNS)

  Recommendation: That the City Council (1) open the public hearing and take testimony
  on proposed Ordinance No. 741; (2) close the public hearing; and (3) introduce for first
  reading Ordinance No. 741.

CITY ATTORNEY DAVIS stated that the draft ordinance was discussed at the City Council
workshop in April and was presented to the Planning Commission in June; there have been
no changes since. He stated that the redlined changes were procedural changes and
clarifications, which included expanding institutional signs and relaxing the regulation on
window signage in the commercial area. He also stated that there was a change in the
temporary sign regulation, clarifying that properties may have two signs with non-commercial
messages.

  MAYOR PRO TEM HUFF moved, seconded by COUNCIL MEMBER STEGURA to,

  OPEN THE PUBLIC HEARING

  There being no objection, MAYOR ZERUNYAN so moved.

Public comment was invited via email, via eComment on the City’s website, and during the live
Zoom Webinar as noticed on the Agenda and on the City’s website and social media platforms.

CITY COUNCIL MINUTES  3
MAY 24, 2022
 No public testimony was received.

  COUNCIL MEMBER STEGURA moved, seconded by MAYOR PRO TEM HUFF to,

  CLOSE THE PUBLIC HEARING

  There being no objection, MAYOR ZERUNYAN so moved.

  COUNCIL MEMBER STEGURA moved, seconded by MAYOR PRO TEM HUFF TO
  APPROVE AS FOLLOWS BY THE FOLLOWING ROLL CALL VOTE:

  APPROVE THE INTRODUCTION OF ORDINANCE NO. 741, AMENDING AND
  RESTATING MUNICIPAL CODE CHAPTER 17.60 (SIGNS) BY THE
  FOLLOWING ROLL CALL VOTE:

  AYES:  Zuckerman, Stegura, Huff, Zerunyan
  ABSENT:  Schmitz

8.  NEW BUSINESS
A.  PARK AND ACTIVITIES COMMISSION ACTION ITEM FROM MEETING OF APRIL
  18, 2022: PLAY STRUCTURE AT CHANDLER PARK

  Recommendation: That the City Council approve the concept of installing small play
  equipment at Chandler Park with attention to equestrian safety which will contemplate
  placement of the equipment, possible fencing and brush clearance as needed, and
  signage to help educate the public on horse safety for visitors as well as signage for
  riders on nearby trail; and direct staff to further study the concept which could include
  ADA analysis of the park and a future conceptual design.

MAYOR ZERUNYAN stated that the City Council received email correspondence from
constituents on this item.

Assistant City Manager Davis provided a presentation summarizing the staff report (as per the
agenda material).

In response to questions by MAYOR PRO TEM HUFF, Assistant City Manager Davis
confirmed that the Equestrian Committee opposed this project when it was initially presented,
and this was conveyed to the Park and Activities Commission, who decided to do further
analysis with a subcommittee that represented the Equestrian Committee and community
members. She stated that the committee is generally concerned with the play equipment and
to make sure safety is considered for equestrians. She further added that other concerns are
that the play equipment is too close to the arena or to the trail.

COUNCIL MEMBER STEGURA commented on the survey results and expressed concern
with the installation of the play equipment in that park and in the proposed location, due to
concerns for the safety of the equestrians who use the park.

COUNCIL MEMBER ZUCKERMAN commented on the survey results and expressed his
concern with safety and asked if there has been any discussion on children walking to the park.
Assistant City Manager Davis stated that a lot of the discussion was regarding access from
North of Palos Verdes Drive North; however, there is a crosswalk on Palos Verdes Drive North
at the City Hall entrance.

COUNCIL MEMBER ZUCKERMAN commented that the proposed play equipment is not that
compelling and questioned whether the equipment is going to be popular.

Lyneigh Palacios, Resident on Palos Verdes Drive North, thanked the city on providing the
technology to participate in this meeting virtually. Ms. Palacios stated that she is in support of
the request to install play equipment at Chandler Park and is advocating for children and their
caregivers and to support families in the community. She asked that the City Council to
approve the request to develop conceptual plans to install play equipment, with two
amendments, 1) remove the maximum space allowed for the play equipment, and 2) that the

CITY COUNCIL MINUTES  4
MAY 24, 2022
 play equipment picked be mindful of the needs of five-year old children.

Rick and Chris Oldroyd, Residents at 40 Ranchview, stated that they are opposed to this
project because they would like to maintain the green open space. They expressed their
concern with the additional needs for installing fencing, brush clearance, and signage in order
to install a few pieces of play equipment. In addition, they commented that it may be quite
expensive to bring this to ADA compliance.

Pam Schachter, Resident, stated that she was a member of the subcommittee and
commended City staff on their work with the survey. Mrs. Schachter commented that she would
like to maintain the green open space and expressed her concern with safety.

Jim Marziani, Resident on Roanwood Drive, stated that Chandler Park is in the heart of the
City’s horse overlay zone. He stated that at the April 19th Park and Activities Commission
meeting there were two in favor and seven opposed to this project, and there was extensive
discussion on how easily horses are spooked. Mr. Marziani commented that everyone is
welcome at this park and asked that the City Council stop spending time and money
researching this item.

Ryan McCormick, Park and Activities Commission member, stated that as a Commissioner,
he would like to see the overall enjoyment of the park. He stated that the Commission felt that
it was appropriate for the scope of use within the small footprint of this park. He added that the
noise would be from the children and people in general since the proposed play equipment
makes no noise.

COUNCIL MEMBER STEGURA stated that reading the comments in the survey, everyone
who identified themselves as equestrian were opposed to this project. Commissioner
McCormick stated that he also attended the subcommittee meeting and guessed that about
65% of equestrians were opposed to this project, but there were some who felt there was room
for compromise.

MAYOR PRO TEM HUFF stated that there are strong arguments on both sides. She stated
that she is concerned with representing the city and the interest of the residents as well as
concerns about safety.

COUNCIL MEMBER ZUCKERMAN asked with respect to the ADA survey, whether the play
equipment makes a difference. Assistant City Manager Davis confirmed that an ADA analysis
of the park will need to be done regardless of this project.

MAYOR ZERUNYAN stated that he does not want this to be characterized as equestrian
against children. He questioned the difference between children playing at the park and
children playing on noiseless equipment. He suggested that staff explore other options for the
play equipment and addressing the needs of the community.

In response to a question by COUNCIL MEMBER ZUCKERMAN, Assistant City Manager
Davis stated that there has not been an assessment of placing the play equipment in another
location since the idea was to keep the equipment away from the arena. However, she stated
that there may another location that can be discussed.

City Manager Grammer stated that the ADA analysis needs to be done and the placement of
the play equipment could be part of this analysis.

There was consensus among the City Council to bring this item back after the ADA analysis.

B.  ANNUAL AUDIT SERVICES AGREEMENT

  Recommendation: That the City Council approve the agreement per City Attorney’s
  approval and rates for the CPA firm of Rogers, Anderson, Malody & Scott, LLP to
  perform the annual audit and report for the Fiscal Year 2021-22, perform the single
  audit, prepare the Pepper Tree Foundation’s tax returns, and review the GANN
  appropriation limitation.

Director Whitehead summarized the staff report (as per the agenda material).

CITY COUNCIL MINUTES  5
MAY 24, 2022
 MAYOR PRO TEM HUFF asked for clarification regarding the $4,605 for the single audit in
addition to the $43K annual audit. Director Whitehead stated that the single audit is a separate
audit and is added to the annual audit.

  MAYOR PRO TEM HUFF moved, seconded by COUNCIL MEMBER STEGURA TO

D.  PLANNING APPLICATION NO. 220194 ZONING CODE UPDATES TO BE
  CONSISTENT WITH THE GENERAL PLAN 2040 COMMUNITY BENEFIT DENSITY
  PROGRAM LOCATION: CITYWIDE

  Recommendation: That the City Council consider the high-level overall structure of the
  program and its components, discuss the issues, and direct staff to further develop the
  framework for the Community Benefit Density program for additional discussion at a

CITY COUNCIL MINUTES  6
MAY 24, 2022
   future meeting. Attachments: Staff Report

Planning Manager Naughton provided a presentation summarizing the staff report (as per the
agenda material).

The following comments were made regarding Community Benefits:

MAYOR ZERUNYAN suggested affordable units as a community benefit.

MAYOR ZERUNYAN emphasized that regarding community benefits, he would like to make
sure that these are directional and inspirational in nature and to not deprive this City Council
or future Councils from the opportunity to weigh the cost to benefit analysis in granting
entitlements.

COUNCIL MEMBER STEGURA suggested workforce housing as a community benefit, which
may also be affordable housing. She added that this is something that can be done for first
responders.

City Manager Grammer clarified that the State density bonus of up to 50% would be given for
affordable housing, which would be an additional incentive for affordable housing.

COUNCIL MEMBER ZUCKERMAN stated that there are already incentives for affordable
housing in State law and does not know if he would want to go beyond that. He asked if the
focus could be on certain areas, such as the Promenade where density bonus could be
granted at this location only. He added that art should not be a part of this since it is so
subjective.

Planning Manager Naughton clarified that currently 30 units/acre are allowed; if a developer
met the requirements of the State density bonus law, they could get up to 50%; and, if a
developer met the maximum criteria of this program, they could get an additional 50%, with a
maximum of 68 units/acre.

City Attorney Davis stated that the location can be selected by way of a General Plan and
Zoning Code amendment. He added that an applicant would need to make this request for a
specific property.

In response to a question by COUNCIL MEMBER ZUCKERMAN, Planning Manager
Naughton stated that if someone were to propose a hotel, the hotel component would be part
of a mixed-use development where the developer is also proposing a residential development.
The density bonus would apply to the residential development.

City Manager Grammer clarified that projects would be reviewed on a case-by-case basis and
there would be development agreements for each of these projects.

The following comments were made regarding Off-site Improvements:

MAYOR ZERUNYAN stated that off-site improvements should be reviewed on a case-by-case
basis.

COUNCIL MEMBER ZUCKERMAN stated that one example would be a parking structure.

COUNCIL MEMBER STEGURA concurred with the Mayor’s comments and added that, since
there is a housing shortage and State-imposed housing requirements, there is a need to attract
developers to build housing and get a fair rate of return. She suggested off-site improvements
to help develop trails, a nature center, a parklet, or park equipment. She also clarified that the
City Council is not looking for a blanket 68 unit/acre goal for the city and rather a ceiling for a
project that is the right fit for the city.

The following comments were made regarding the Program Structure:

Planning Manager Naughton stated that the challenge is how to quantify the percentage bonus
density to the proposed benefit of improvement. She provided a brief example of the State’s
Density Law Bonus percentages.

CITY COUNCIL MINUTES  7
MAY 24, 2022
 City Attorney Davis explained that the State’s “very low income” percentage will provide for a
50% density bonus, so there is no incentive for any percentage above 15%. He emphasized
that due to this issue with the State’s Density Bonus Law, workforce housing could work.

Planning Manager Naughton stated that four program structures were discussed internally,
which included a fixed percentage that may be problematic; pro-forma analysis provided by
the applicant; economic analysis/appraisal, which would be retained by the city at the
applicant’s expense; and a site-by-site analysis, which would look at the unique circumstances
of particular sites.

MAYOR ZERUNYAN stated that the program structure would need to be a combination of
pro-forma, economic analysis/appraisal, and a site-by-site analysis.

The following comments were made regarding implementation:

Planning Manager Naughton stated that staff is proposing to incorporate the Community
Benefit Density Program as part of a Development Agreement Resolution. This would include
a preliminary review of the community benefits and the project scope. Additionally, the
development agreement would run concurrently with the entitlement process and CEQA.

In response to a question by Council Member Zuckerman, Planning Manager Naughton stated
that the preliminary review of community benefits and the project scope would be brought
before the City Council. City Attorney Davis explained that the preliminary review is a
mechanism for the Council to sign off on a project without making a commitment.

Planning Manager Naughton stated that this is part of the Title 17 Zoning Code Update to be
consistent with the updated General Plan. Additionally, the Density Bonus and Other
Incentives Chapter in the Municipal Code will also be updated. She also stated that the
Community Benefit Density Program will come back to the City Council for further review prior
to drafting an ordinance.

CITY COUNCIL directed staff to further develop the framework for the Community Benefit
Density Program for additional discussion at a future meeting.
